name: Shoulder turn-out
movement: elbow bent at the side, the forearm turned outward away from the body and back

phone.placement: Stand the phone up on the floor, two or three metres away, facing you. Stand square to it.

words.hint: Facing the phone, elbow tucked at the side and bent to a right angle, the forearm swung outward.
words.start: Stand the phone up on the floor. Stand facing it, the working elbow tucked at your side, bent square, hand forward.
words.position: Stand facing the phone. Tuck the working elbow in against your side and bend it to a right angle, the forearm pointing straight at the phone. A rolled towel between elbow and ribs helps keep it there.
words.top: The forearm turned outward, away from the body, as far as is comfortable — the elbow still against the side, the chest still facing the phone.
howto: Elbow against your side, bent to a right angle, hand pointing at the phone. Hold a band in both hands if you have one.
Keeping the elbow pinned, turn the forearm outward, away from your body, as far as is comfortable — a few inches at first.
Hold for the count with the chest still facing the phone.
Turn back slowly. The rep counts when the hand is pointing forward again.
words.cannot: The shoulder joint itself: it reads the turn from how much of the forearm the camera sees, the elbow leaving the side and the chest turning. Keep the elbow pinned yourself.
words.about: Shoulder turn-out — facing the phone: the turn, as the elbow-to-wrist length the camera sees against the upper arm, as a percent — a forearm pointing at the phone is foreshortened to almost nothing, one turned fully out to the side shows its whole length (about 100); the top is at least 50 (a quarter turn); a rep is under way past 30 and counts when back under 20. The elbow kept in, as the elbow-to-hip distance against the trunk at most 45%; the elbow bent to 70–110°; and the chest facing the phone, as the shoulder width at least 85% of what it was at the start — turning the body narrows it. Hold two seconds. A frozen shoulder manages a few inches: set the top low and raise it.
words.lost: Stand facing the camera, both arms in the picture
words.early: Hold it at the top next time
words.safety: Gentle: this is the direction a frozen shoulder loses first. A band should be light.
words.easier: A smaller turn; no band; a shorter hold.
words.harder: A heavier band; a longer hold; a further turn.
words.mistakes: The elbow drifting away from the side; turning the whole body instead of the arm; the elbow straightening; the shoulder hiking.

measurements.label: forearm seen, % of upper arm
measurements.why: The elbow-to-wrist length as the camera sees it, against the upper arm: pointing at the phone it is foreshortened to 10–30; turned fully out to the side it shows its whole length, about 100. Also the progress measurement.

settings.label: Forearm seen at the top, % of the upper arm, at least

measurements.label: elbow from the hip, % of trunk
measurements.why: The elbow-to-hip distance against the trunk: an elbow against the ribs sits around 30; drifting out to the side it grows. Past 45 it has left the side.

settings.label: Elbow from the hip, % of the trunk, at most

measurements.label: elbow bent
measurements.why: The elbow at a right angle, 70–110: straighter and the band is being pushed rather than the shoulder turned.

measurements.label: shoulder width, % of start
measurements.why: The shoulder width against the hip width, as a percent of what it was at the start: turning the chest away from the phone narrows it. Under 85 the body is turning instead of the arm.

settings.label: Shoulder width, % of the start, at least

faults.label: Elbow opening
faults.text: Keep the elbow bent to a right angle

faults.label: Turn short
faults.text: Turn the forearm out a little further
faults.deep: Further out if you can, to the point of stretch

faults.label: Elbow leaving the side
faults.text: Keep the elbow tucked in at your side
faults.deep: The elbow has come away from your side — pin it to your ribs

faults.label: Body turning
faults.text: Keep the chest facing the phone — turn the arm, not your body
